title: Why does everyone love Dolly Parton?
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the show's iHeart announcer chiming in) explore why Dolly Parton is so widely beloved. They cover her upbringing in a crowded two-room Smoky Mountains cabin, early start in music under Uncle Bill Owens, her years with Porter Wagoner, her move into solo and crossover pop-country success with hits like "Jolene," "I Will Always Love You," and "Here You Come Again," her songwriting, TV and film work, the founding of Dollywood, her political neutrality and public stances, her philanthropy (Dollywood Foundation literacy program, COVID-19 vaccine research donation), her business savvy and music catalog, and her awards and recognition. The episode closes with listener mail about a grandmother's Pac-Man skills.
topics: Dolly Parton business and music catalog

segments.title: Opening banter and tour plug
segments.summary: The hosts plug upcoming tour dates in DC, Boston, and Toronto, then introduce the episode title question of why everyone loves Dolly Parton and praise her consistency and political neutrality.

segments.title: Why people love Dolly Parton
segments.summary: The hosts offer hypotheses: she is likable from all sides, avoids hot-button politics, and seems genuine. They note she is rarely disliked and has broad cross-political appeal.

segments.title: Childhood in the Smoky Mountains
segments.summary: Dolly Parton was born January 19, 1946, in rural Tennessee, the fourth of twelve children. The family of fourteen lived in a two-room cabin without running water or electricity, and she had a relatively free childhood.

segments.title: Early musical start and Grand Ole Opry debut
segments.summary: Her granddad was a Pentecostal minister and she has a personal faith. Uncle Bill Owens nurtured her early musical interest. She wrote a first song around age five, recorded Puppy Love in 1959, and made her Grand Ole Opry debut at thirteen, introduced by Johnny Cash.

segments.title: Moving to Nashville and meeting Carl Dean
segments.summary: Dolly debuted on Mercury Records in 1962 and moved to Nashville the day after graduating high school. She met Carl Dean at a laundromat, and they married in 1966. Carl Dean avoids the spotlight and runs an asphalt business.

segments.title: Fan interactions and her flirty persona
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Dolly treats public time as belonging to fans and keeps leisure time private with Carl. They note her playful flirtatious persona, which Carl understands.

segments.title: Personal connections to Dolly Parton's music
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh share how they were introduced to Dolly through family, including her father and Chuck's parents, and the film Nine to Five.

segments.title: Monument Records debut and first albums
segments.summary: Monument Records wanted her to be a pop singer, but she insisted on country. Her first album, Hello, I'm Dolly (1967), had top twenty country hits including Something Fishy, which she wrote.

segments.title: Working with Porter Wagoner
segments.summary: Porter Wagoner hired Dolly for his TV show, which became the top syndicated show. They recorded duets, including Just Between You and Me in 1968. Wagoner controlled her through restrictive contracts. Their breakup inspired I Will Always Love You, and they reconciled before his death.

segments.title: Songwriting for I Will Always Love You and solo breakout
segments.summary: Dolly reportedly wrote I Will Always Love You and Jolene around the same time. She released many albums between 1968 and 1973 and got out of her Wagoner contract. She also left her family band and built her own band.

segments.title: Dolly TV show, Sandy Gallin, and crossover pop success
segments.summary: Dolly hosted a TV variety show in 1976-77. Manager Sandy Gallin booked her at the Bottom Line in New York, got her touring Europe, and was gay, which helped build her LGBTQ fan base. Here You Come Again became a crossover hit, reaching number one on country and number three on pop charts.

segments.title: TV circuit, 1980s collaborations, and Christmas albums
segments.summary: Dolly made hundreds of TV appearances to become a household name. She collaborated with Kenny Rogers on Islands in the Stream and with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris on the 1987 album Trio. The hosts discuss her bluegrass and Christmas albums, including Once Upon a Christmas and A Holly Dolly Christmas.

segments.title: Songwriting, instruments, and Glastonbury
segments.summary: Dolly considers songwriting her greatest pride and often writes from a male point of view. She plays guitar, banjo, fiddle, and saxophone, and her 2014 Glastonbury appearance boosted her UK fame.

segments.title: Nine to Five movie and Miley Cyrus connection
segments.summary: The 1980 film Nine to Five was based on the early-1970s Nine to Five movement, which protested sexual harassment and pay inequity. Dolly's goddaughter Miley Cyrus and her appearances on Hannah Montana helped introduce Dolly to millennials. Other films include Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, Steel Magnolias, Rhinestone, and Straight Talk, and the production company with Sandy Gallin produced Father of the Bride and Buffy the Vampire Slayer.

segments.title: Transition to Dollywood
segments.summary: The hosts pause before turning to Dollywood, which began with a 1982 Barbara Walters interview in which Dolly mentioned wanting a theme park back home.

segments.title: Dollywood origins and opening
segments.summary: Jack and Pete Hershend, owners of Silver Dollar City in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, heard the interview and partnered with her. Dollywood opened four years later, and its first year drew 1.3 million visitors. A time capsule with an unreleased song is reportedly set to open when she is ninety-nine.

segments.title: Visiting Dollywood and nearby attractions
segments.summary: Josh describes Dollywood's coal-fired train, candle dipping, food, and its museum showing the original Coat of Many Colors and her lists and wigs. The hosts also discuss roller coasters and the nearby Lee Greenwood Cafe and Gatlinburg attractions.

segments.title: Anthropologists, sociologists, and global fandom
segments.summary: Sociologist Tracy McMillan Cotttom wrote that Black women admire Dolly as a role model. Her Q score is among the highest, and her low negative Q score shows she is broadly liked. Anthropologist Jonathan Zilberg wrote about her popularity in Zimbabwe, and Nelson Mandela reportedly had jailers play her music in prison.

segments.title: Politics, humor, feminism, and social stances
segments.summary: Dolly avoids endorsing politicians and jokes about her body. She writes dark songs about women's struggles, such as Daddy Come and Get Me from 1970. She considers herself pro-women rather than a movement feminist, supported Black Lives Matter, and renamed Dixie Stampede to Dolly Parton Stampede in 2018.

segments.title: Business savvy, catalog, and philanthropy
segments.summary: Dolly kept her songwriting rights and turned down Elvis Presley's request for half of I Will Always Love You publishing. Her catalog is reportedly worth about $150 million, and she licenses her image for products. Her Dollywood Foundation promotes literacy, and she donated $1 million to Vanderbilt for COVID-19 vaccine research.

segments.title: Awards, recognition, and new album
segments.summary: Dolly has 53 Grammy nominations and ten wins, plus an Emmy and two Oscar nominations. She holds two Guinness World Records and two Hollywood Walk of Fame stars. She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and has a new album, Rock Star, coming out.
topics: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame

segments.title: Closing thoughts on Dolly Parton
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up their Dolly Parton discussion, joke about additional facts, and mention her interview skills, which lead to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: grandmother and Pac-Man
segments.summary: Listener Aaron Miller of Kansas City shares that his traditional grandmother secretly played Pac-Man and reached the level 256 kill screen before he saw it documented in King of Kong.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The iHeart announcer closes the episode and promotes iHeartRadio podcasts.
